one_liner: Header-only, single-file open-addressing hash map/set beating std::unordered_map on speed and memory.
what_it_does: robin_hood::unordered_map and robin_hood::unordered_set are single-header, largely drop-in replacements for std::unordered_map/std::unordered_set, built on open addressing with Robin Hood displacement instead of separate chaining. Two layouts are exposed directly: unordered_flat_map stores key/value pairs inline in one array (fastest, no reference/pointer stability), and unordered_node_map indirects through a custom bulk allocator to keep pointer/reference stability similar to std::unordered_map. The unordered_map/unordered_set aliases pick flat vs. node layout heuristically based on value size.
how_it_is_fast: Open addressing with Robin Hood hashing bounds probe-sequence-length variance, and backward-shift deletion removes the need for tombstones, so there's no per-node allocation or pointer chasing on the hot path. Each slot carries a 1-byte 'info' field packing probe distance plus hoisted hash bits, so most negative lookups are rejected without a full key comparison; the flat layout keeps keys/values contiguous for cache locality. A custom robin_hood::hash (multiply-shift avalanche, specialized fast paths for integers and std::string) is used by default; the node variant additionally uses a bulk pool allocator to avoid per-insert malloc calls. No SIMD is used — it's portable scalar C++ relying on bit-scan intrinsics, not vector instructions.
when_to_use: Hot-path integer- or string-keyed maps/sets where insert/erase/find throughput dominates and you use robin_hood::hash (or another well-mixed hash)
Large bulk workloads (tens of millions of entries) where std::unordered_map's per-node allocation and pointer chasing dominate runtime and RSS
You want a drop-in std::unordered_map-shaped API without rewriting call sites: unordered_flat_map for max speed, unordered_node_map when pointer/reference stability is required
Header-only vendoring is acceptable (single ~2500-line file, MIT) and you're fine freezing on an unmaintained snapshot
C++11/14/17/20 codebase, including non-x86/non-AVX platforms, since the implementation is portable scalar C++
when_not_to_use: You need iterator stability across inserts — neither variant guarantees it, and unordered_flat_map also invalidates references/pointers on rehash

You rely on a poorly-mixed or identity hash for integer keys (e.g. libstdc++'s default std::hash<int>) — the record's own caveats note robin_hood times out in several benchmarks without its own hash, and a badly mixed hash can make insert throw std::overflow_error
Your workload spikes memory and then shrinks — unordered_node_map's bulk allocator never returns freed blocks to the OS for the life of the map, so peak RSS persists (GitHub issue #107)
You need heterogeneous/transparent lookup (e.g. find by string_view into a map<std::string,...>) — attempts to use it hit unresolved problems per an open issue (#80)

You need active maintenance, custom-allocator support, or a cheap operator= — the repo is archived since 2023 (author recommends ankerl::unordered_dense), custom allocators aren't supported (issue #136, closed unimplemented), and copy-assignment has an open perf bug where it frees then reallocates instead of reusing the buffer (issue #149)

integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (header explicitly targets 11/14/17/20; the project's own CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD to 14)
integration.platforms: any (portable scalar C++, no SIMD/AVX requirement); README states 'platform independent' and CI badges cover Linux/macOS (Travis) and Windows (AppVeyor)
integration.thread_safety: not documented — no internal synchronization visible in the header; treat like std::unordered_map (safe for concurrent reads only, external locking required for any write)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same map/set method surface as std::unordered_map, but unordered_flat_map gives up reference/pointer stability, and with a badly-mixed hash insert can throw std::overflow_error where std::unordered_map would simply degrade in performance

gotchas: unordered_node_map's bulk allocator never frees memory back to the OS during the map's lifetime — a one-time size spike leaves RSS elevated until the map is destroyed (issue #107)
A sufficiently bad/adversarial hash can make insert throw std::overflow_error instead of degrading gracefully like std::unordered_map (README 'Design Choices' section)
Heterogeneous/transparent lookup via is_transparent hash+equal does not work as expected in practice (issue #80, open)
copy-assignment (operator=) frees all memory and reallocates from scratch rather than reusing the existing buffer (issue #149, open)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick robin_hood over abseil::flat_hash_map, Boost.Unordered, or folly::F14 when you want a single dependency-free header to vendor and can't pull in Abseil/Boost/Folly; for any new project, the author's own successor ankerl::unordered_dense is the better default since robin_hood is explicitly unmaintained and unordered_dense is the sibling entry it was retired in favor of.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's 2019 map_benchmark suite (g++ 8.2.0, -O3 -march=native, libstdc++ std::unordered_map as baseline, Intel Core i7-8700 @3.2GHz locked), robin_hood::unordered_flat_map inserted+erased 100M int pairs in 16.9s using 1717MB vs. std::unordered_map's 99.7s / 3986MB (5.9x faster, ~2.3x less peak memory), both using robin_hood::hash; robin_hood::unordered_node_map took 45.5s / 2293MB (2.2x faster). Numbers are first-party, from a 2019-era g++ 8.2/libstdc++ toolchain.
status_note: Abandoned: the author stopped development (last commit 2023-04-21, repo carries a 'deprecated' issue template) and publicly recommends migrating to ankerl::unordered_dense, but it's MIT-licensed and small enough (one header) to vendor and freeze indefinitely.
